items.summary: A flaw was found in Cockpit. An unauthenticated remote attacker can exploit this vulnerability by initiating and sustaining numerous simultaneous connections to the `cockpit-tls` service. This forces the service to create an unbounded number of detached threads, consuming system resources such as memory and file descriptors. The primary consequence is a denial of service (DoS), leading to degradation or complete unavailability of the Cockpit service for legitimate users.

items.summary: A missing authorization check has been found in the find_user function in user_aware.rb of the SSH key API in the foreman package. The create action attaches a new public key to the user id in the request without checking that the caller may edit that user. A low-privileged network attacker or user who already holds permission to create SSH keys can add their key to another user's account. That key is then stored with the victim and can be used by features that export that user's SSH keys.

A flaw was found in ansible-core's ansible.builtin.git module. The module
invokes git (ls-remote, clone, fetch) with the repository URL as a positional
argument and without a "--" separator, so a repository URL that begins with a
dash is interpreted by git as a command-line option. A caller that passes an
attacker-controlled repository URL to the module can trigger argument
injection (for example --upload-pack/--exec), resulting in arbitrary command
execution on the host running the module.

items.summary:
The fix for CVE-2026-45756 lowers pcre.backtrack_limit to 10000 around each preg_match() call of the match() and search() filter functions. That limit applies to one starting position, not to one call. PCRE resets its counter at every position it tries a match from. So an unanchored pattern that stays just under the limit is paid once per byte of the subject. Each call also starts from a fresh limit, so chaining clauses in one filter multiplies the work.

Two other paths made the cost of a query grow faster than its size, without any regular expression:
- The filter evaluator scanned the whole expression for logical operators once per node. Its cost grew with the square of the number of chained clauses.
- Queries starting with $ inside a filter, like @.x == $.limit or length($.items), were evaluated again for every node the filter visits.

An application that evaluates an attacker-influenced JSONPath expression can therefore still be made to hold a PHP worker. A document of 2 MB and a query of 2.5 KB take 3.5 minutes of CPU.

JsonCrawler::find() now bounds the total regex work of one call, and throws an exception when that budget is exhausted. Filter expressions are parsed once per query, and absolute queries inside filters are evaluated once per query.

items.summary:
Most methods of Symfony\Component\Filesystem\Path rely on Path::split(), which takes everything before the first :// as the root of a path. It doesn't check that this prefix is a URI scheme, so the .. segments in that prefix are never resolved. PHP sees a scheme only at the start of a string. So /base/../x://../secret.txt is a plain local path to /secret.txt for PHP, while Path::isBasePath('/base', '/base/../x://../secret.txt') returns true. canonicalize(), join(), makeAbsolute() and makeRelative() are affected the same way.

Some applications check a path built from user input with isBasePath() or canonicalize(), and then open it. They can be made to read or write files outside the expected directory.

On Symfony 6.4 and later, the AssetMapper component builds with Path::join() the path of the files that a remote package references from its CSS. A malicious or compromised package can therefore make importmap:require or importmap:install write a file of its choice outside assets/vendor. For example, the CSS url(../../../../../public/x://shell.php) writes public/x:/shell.php.

A prefix is now a scheme only when PHP would look for a stream wrapper with that name. That is two or more letters, digits, +, - or ., followed by :// at the start of the path. Other prefixes are regular path segments, and the .. segments after them are resolved. Real schemes such as phar://, file://, vfs:// or compress.zlib:// keep working.

items.summary:
When Request::getBaseUrl() does not find the script name at the start of the request URI, it looks for it further into the path. This supports web servers that rewrite every URL to a front controller in a subdirectory. The base URL then kept everything before the script name, and the client chooses that part. A request URI starting with // or /\ made the base URL start with a host.

With SCRIPT_NAME=/public/index.php, a request for //evil.example/public/index.php/login is routed to /login, with the base URL //evil.example/public/index.php and the base path //evil.example/public. The URLs generated for that page then point to evil.example:
- links built with path() and the actions of forms, so a login form sends the credentials of the user to evil.example;
- redirects to generated URLs, such as the ones of redirectToRoute();
- assets referenced with a relative path through asset(), so the page can load scripts from evil.example.

The attacker has to make a user follow a crafted link, such as https://app.example//evil.example/public/index.php/login. framework.trusted_hosts does not help, since the host of the request is the real one.

Applications are affected when their front controller is in a subdirectory and the web server sends it URIs that do not start with that directory. A .htaccess file at the root of the project that rewrites every URL to public/ does that, for instance.

Applications are also affected when the web server sets SCRIPT_NAME to the path of the request. Some nginx configurations do that when they send every request to the front controller without fastcgi_split_path_info. php -S does it too, with a router script outside the document root. A request for /\evil.example/index.php then gets the base URL /\evil.example/index.php, which browsers read as a link to evil.example.

The configurations recommended in the Symfony documentation are not affected.

Request::getBaseUrl() now returns an empty base URL when the request URI starts with // or /\.

items.summary:
Since the fix for CVE-2025-64500, Request::getPathInfo() strips the script name from the start of the URL. It does so even when the script name is only the start of a longer path segment. With SCRIPT_NAME set to /index.php, a request to /index.phpadmin gets the path info /admin and is routed like /admin. Encoded spellings such as /index%2Ephpadmin or /%69ndex.phpadmin work too. Before that fix, the path info was admin, which no route matched.

Rules enforced by Symfony are not affected: access_control and firewalls read the same path info as the router. Rules enforced in front of PHP are. The nginx configuration of the Symfony documentation and the .htaccess file of symfony/apache-pack make /index.php/admin unreachable, but they pass /index.phpadmin to the front controller. So a location /admin block in nginx, a <Location /admin> section in Apache, or a CDN or WAF rule on /admin can be bypassed.

The script name is now stripped only when it is followed by /, ? or the end of the URL. A request to /index.phpadmin gets the path info /index.phpadmin.

items.summary: A flaw was found in the GLib DMA-BUF path of WebKitGTK. The UIProcess trusted fds.size() as the DMA-BUF plane count when handling AcceleratedBackingStore::DidCreateDMABufBuffer and copied offsets and strides without verifying that those vectors had the same length. A compromised WebProcess can send mismatched vector lengths, causing an out-of-bounds read in the privileged UIProcess. This can disclose UIProcess memory and crash the UIProcess, and may be used as part of a Web Content sandbox-escape chain.

items.summary:
The controllers.json loader of @symfony/stimulus-bridge loads the package.json file of each package listed in controllers.json with require(). Node resolves this path through the exports field of the package, which can map ./package.json to a script. require() then runs that script during the Webpack or Symfony Encore build.

This is a build-time vulnerability: it doesn't affect browsers or end users. A malicious or compromised package listed in controllers.json can run code on the developer machine or the CI server. This works even when the package manager doesn't run install scripts. This code can read the files and environment variables of the build, like CI secrets, and change the built assets.

The loader now reads the resolved file and parses it as JSON, so that a mapped script fails to parse instead of running.

items.summary:
The @symfony/stimulus-bridge npm package includes a Webpack loader called lazy-controller-loader that supports "magic comments" placed above a Stimulus controller import, for example /* stimulusFetch: 'lazy' */, to control lazy loading behavior. To read those options, the loader extracted the raw text of any stimulus* comment and evaluated it as JavaScript using Node's vm.runInNewContext(). The Node.js node:vm module is not a security sandbox, and a crafted comment can break out of the VM context using well-known techniques to run arbitrary Node.js code within the build process.

This is a build-time vulnerability: it does not affect browsers or end users. The code executes on the developer machine or CI/build server during a Webpack or Symfony Encore build. Realistic attack vectors include a malicious Stimulus controller introduced through a compromised dependency, or a pull request that triggers an automated CI build. An attacker who can get such a file into the build can read files and environment variables available to the build process, exfiltrate CI secrets, tamper with generated build artifacts, and run commands with the permissions of the build user.

The loader no longer evaluates comment content as JavaScript. It now parses each comment as an object expression using a real JavaScript parser and extracts only plain literal values. Any non-literal value, such as a function call, an identifier, or a sequence expression, is rejected and reported as a build error instead of being executed. Legitimate option values like 'lazy' and 'eager' continue to work without any changes required on the user's side.

items.summary:
The fix for CVE-2026-55877 (GHSA-6v8j-33hc-mv84) sanitizes the SVG of icons before they are rendered inline. The checks matched attribute names as written in the icon, while browsers and the renderer read some names differently.

On 2.x, fromFile() keys the attributes of the root <svg> element by their local name. A handler like x:onload passed the check, and was then rendered as onload, which runs on load. HTML parsers also read attribute names case-insensitively, so a SMIL animation with ATTRIBUTENAME="href" could set a javascript: URL on a link. And an href in the XLink namespace under another prefix, like q:href, wasn't checked. On 3.x, the sanitizer writes it out as xlink:href, and XML parsers resolve the prefix on both branches.

Applications are exposed when an attacker can influence the SVG of the icons they render. The sources are the same as for CVE-2026-55877, like local icon files and the responses of the Iconify API.

The sanitizer now checks attributes by local name. It also finds the attributeName of animations in any case, and ignores the prefix of its value.

#[AsLiveComponent(route: '...')] makes a live component send its requests to another route. The documentation suggests it so that the component lives under a specific firewall, for example. The default /_components/{_live_component}/{_live_action} route still served the component, though. A request to it rendered the component and ran its actions outside the firewall and the access rules of the configured route.

The request needs props signed by the application, which a page that rendered the component provides. Controller attributes on the component, like #[IsGranted], still applied.

A live component is now only served by the route it is configured with.

The fix for CVE-2026-55877 (GHSA-6v8j-33hc-mv84) sanitizes the SVG of icons before they are rendered inline. Browsers parse an inline

, or . They then parse the rest of the icon as HTML, and they also parse the content of and <desc> elements as HTML. The sanitizer only checked icons as SVG, so an icon could contain markup that becomes live once parsed as HTML. For example, after a <p> element, a comment can end a <style> element early and add an <img> element with an event handler: <p/><style><!--</style><img src=1 onerror=alert(1)>--></style> In the same way, an icon could add a <base> element to the page, which changes where its relative links and forms go. It could also add a <meta> element that redirects the page. Comments were kept too, while browsers end a comment at <!--> or <!--->. The rest of such a comment then became live markup, even without any HTML element before it. Applications are exposed when an attacker can influence the SVG of the icons they render. The sources are the same as for CVE-2026-55877, like local icon files and the responses of the Iconify API. The sanitizer now removes comments and the elements that make browsers switch to HTML, and only keeps the text of <title> and <desc> elements. It also makes sure that markup in CDATA sections and attribute values can't end a <noscript> element around the icon.

items.summary:
The fix for CVE-2026-55877 (GHSA-6v8j-33hc-mv84) sanitizes the SVG of icons before they are rendered inline. When the sanitizer changes an icon, it writes the icon out again as HTML. HTML writes the content of some elements, like <style>, without escaping it. But inside an <svg>, browsers parse the content of a <style> element as markup. Escaped markup in such an element then becomes live in the page:

<path onclick="x"/><style xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"><img src=x onerror=alert(1)></style>

The event handler of the <path> element only makes the sanitizer change the icon. Depending on the version, this affects every <style> element, or the elements of the XHTML namespace, like <style>, <xmp> or <noembed>.

On 2.x, the elements of the XHTML namespace were also kept. An XHTML <form> or <base> element then becomes live where icons are parsed as XML, like in the Google Maps bridge of ux-map.

Applications are exposed when an attacker can influence the SVG of the icons they render. The sources are the same as for CVE-2026-55877, like local icon files and the responses of the Iconify API.

On 2.x, the sanitizer now writes icons out as XML, which escapes their text, and only keeps the elements of the SVG namespace. On 3.x, it now only keeps the elements of the SVG namespace.

items.summary:
A live component protected by #[IsGranted], on its class or on its default action, can be rendered by a caller who is not granted access. POST /_components/{name}/_batch is handled by Symfony\UX\LiveComponent\Controller\BatchActionController, which has no controller attributes: the attributes of the component are only checked by the sub-request issued for each action. With an empty actions list, no sub-request was issued, and the hydrated component was rendered and returned with a 200.

The caller needs a valid signed props payload for the component, such as the data-live-props-value of a page that rendered it: one the caller could see before losing access, or a cached or shared page. The checksum binds the props to the component name, not to a user, a session or a time, so such a payload can be replayed. Actions are not affected, since each action of a non-empty batch is still checked in its own sub-request. Components that load data from their props, like an entity identifier, disclose that data to the caller.

BatchActionController now rejects a batch without any action with a BadRequestHttpException. The JavaScript client never sends such a request: it uses the URL of the component when there is no action, /{action} for a single one and /_batch for two or more.

items.summary: Reliance on an untrusted source of the client address in the WebSocket listener of the NetBird relay server (relay/server/listener/ws) in NetBird versions 0.31.1 through 0.74.7 allows an attacker with an enrolled peer to spoof the source address of their relay connection. The listener used the values of the X-Real-Ip and X-Real-Port request headers as the remote address of the connection unconditionally, without checking that the request came from a trusted upstream proxy. A WebSocket client that sends both headers makes the relay record and use an arbitrary address for its connection, including in the relay connection log, so a client can hide its real address or attribute its connection to another host. Only the relay server is affected; the NetBird client, including the Android and iOS apps, does not run the relay listener. The issue is fixed in version 0.75.0, which honours these headers only for requests whose direct connection address is in a configured set of trusted proxies and ignores them by default.

items.summary: A protection mechanism failure in the userspace firewall of the NetBird client (client/firewall/uspfilter) in NetBird versions 0.55.0 through 0.74.6 allows an attacker who controls an enrolled peer to bypass the access control rules of another peer by sending IP-fragmented packets. The packet filter returned an allow verdict for any IPv4 fragment, and for any IPv6 packet carrying a Fragment extension header, before evaluating the ACL rules. This applied to the leading fragment as well as to continuation fragments, so no part of a fragmented datagram was filtered and ports denied by policy could be reached. The userspace filter is the packet filter wherever the client does not program the kernel firewall, which includes the Android and iOS apps. The issue is fixed in version 0.74.7, in the Android app from version 0.6.0 and in the iOS app from version 0.3.3, which evaluate fragments against the same ACL rules as unfragmented packets.

items.summary: Deserialization of untrusted data in the relay server handshake of NetBird versions 0.29.0 through 0.74.7 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to reach the Go encoding/gob decoder with attacker-supplied bytes before any credential is checked, which can lead to denial of service of the relay server. The deprecated Hello handshake message was still accepted before authentication and its token was decoded with gob.NewDecoder (shared/relay/auth/hmac) before the HMAC signature was verified. The handshake buffer limits the input to 212 bytes and the pre-authentication phase to 10 seconds, so there is no impact on confidentiality or integrity and the impact on availability depends on a separate weakness in the gob decoder of the Go toolchain used to build the relay server, such as CVE-2024-34156. The Auth handshake, used by clients since version 0.29.1, does not use gob. The issue is fixed in version 0.75.0, which removes the Hello handshake and the gob-based token decoding.

items.summary:
Improper Neutralization of CRLF Sequences vulnerability in ufirstgroup ymlr (Ymlr module) allows attackers to inject arbitrary content into generated YAML documents through document comments. Ymlr.document!/2 interpolates each caller-supplied comment string into the output behind a single # prefix without validating it or escaping line breaks. Because a YAML comment is terminated by a line break, the first carriage return or line feed in the comment string ends the comment context and everything after it is emitted at column 0 of the document body.

An attacker who controls text that the host application passes as a comment can forge top-level mapping keys, override values the application itself set, and emit --- or ... markers that split the output into additional documents. Downstream consumers of the generated YAML, such as configuration loaders, deployment manifests, CI pipelines and data importers, parse the injected content as legitimate data. The same clause backs Ymlr.document/2, Ymlr.documents!/2 and Ymlr.documents/2, so every document encoding entry point is affected.

This vulnerability is associated with program files lib/ymlr.ex and program routines Ymlr.document!/2, Ymlr.documents!/2.

This issue affects ymlr: from 0.0.1 before 5.1.6.

items.summary:
Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in ninenines cowboy allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to exhaust connection process memory over HTTP/1.1.

The HTTP/1.1 handler in cowboy_http enforces the max_headers limit by counting the number of distinct header names in a map (maps:size(Headers)). When a request contains multiple header lines with the same name, the values are concatenated into a single ever-growing binary stored under that one map key (", " for regular headers, "; " for cookies), so the map size stays at one and the max_headers cap (default 100) is never reached. Because no accumulator bounds the total number of header lines or the total byte size of the header block (only per-line max_header_name_length and max_header_value_length apply), an unauthenticated client can send an arbitrary number of header lines with the same name and grow the connection process's binary memory to arbitrary size within the request window.

The impact per connection is bounded by request_timeout (default 5 seconds, not reset by header data), and by max_heap_size when set (the offending connection process is killed once its heap grows past the limit). When max_heap_size is left at the default (unset), sustained abuse can drive the Erlang VM into out-of-memory conditions.

This issue affects cowboy: from 2.0.0-pre.4 before 2.18.0.

items.summary:
Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity vulnerability in mtrudel bandit allows unauthenticated remote denial of service via CPU exhaustion during WebSocket fragment reassembly.

The size guard Bandit.WebSocket.Connection.oversize_message?/2 called from handle_frame/3 in lib/bandit/websocket/connection.ex appends each non-final continuation frame to a left-nested iolist and then re-measures the entire accumulated buffer with IO.iodata_length/1 on every frame. Because the buffer grows by one element per frame and is fully re-traversed each time, reassembly work is quadratic (O(n^2)) in the number of continuation frames.

The max_fragmented_message_size limit (default 8 MB) bounds total bytes but not frame count, and each frame can carry as little as one payload byte, so an attacker can send millions of tiny continuation frames using modest bandwidth to pin a CPU core for minutes to hours. Many concurrent connections can starve the whole server of CPU, denying service to legitimate users. The WebSocket read timeout does not help, because it is an idle timeout evaluated between reads and cannot preempt the synchronous reassembly work spent inside a single callback.

This issue affects bandit: from 1.11.0 before 1.12.1.

items.summary: A flaw was found in Ansible, where sensitive information stored in Ansible Vault files can be exposed in plaintext during the execution of a playbook. This occurs when using tasks such as include_vars to load vaulted variables without setting the no_log: true parameter, resulting in sensitive data being printed in the playbook output or logs. This can lead to the unintentional disclosure of secrets like passwords or API keys, compromising security and potentially allowing unauthorized access or actions.

items.summary: A vulnerability was found in CRI-O, where it can be requested to take a checkpoint archive of a container and later be asked to restore it. When it does that restoration, it attempts to restore the mounts from the restore archive instead of the pod request. As a result, the validations run on the pod spec, verifying that the pod has access to the mounts it specifies are not applicable to a restored container. This flaw allows a malicious user to trick CRI-O into restoring a pod that doesn't have access to host mounts. The user needs access to the kubelet or cri-o socket to call the restore endpoint and trigger the restore.

items.summary: A flaw was found in Aardvark-dns, which is vulnerable to a Denial of Service attack due to the serial processing of TCP DNS queries. An attacker can exploit this flaw by keeping a TCP connection open indefinitely, causing the server to become unresponsive and resulting in other DNS queries timing out. This issue prevents legitimate users from accessing DNS services, thereby disrupting normal operations and causing service downtime.

items.summary: A flaw was found in libvirt. A refactor of the code fetching the list of interfaces for multiple APIs introduced a corner case on platforms where allocating 0 bytes of memory results in a NULL pointer. This corner case would lead to a NULL-pointer dereference and subsequent crash of virtinterfaced. This issue could allow clients connecting to the read-only socket to crash the virtinterfaced daemon.

items.summary: A stack overflow vulnerability exists in the libexpat library due to the way it handles recursive entity expansion in XML documents. When parsing an XML document with deeply nested entity references, libexpat can be forced to recurse indefinitely, exhausting the stack space and causing a crash. This issue could lead to denial of service (DoS) or, in some cases, exploitable memory corruption, depending on the environment and library usage.

This issue may read to a heap-based out-of-bounds writer, impacting grub's sensitive data integrity and eventually leading to a secure boot protection bypass.

However, it fails to properly verify the allocation against possible integer overflows. It's possible to cause the allocation length to overflow with a crafted tar file, leading to a heap out-of-bounds write. This flaw eventually allows an attacker to circumvent secure boot protections.
